copy.headline: Unauthorised access exposes ID numbers of 8.8 million people in Denmark

extended.text: Unauthorised people obtained the names, addresses and personal identification numbers of about 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company's lawful access to the CPR, Denmark's central register of personal data, the digitalisation ministry said on Monday. The misuse lasted about ten days in September. The register holds about 11 million people, including the dead and those who have moved abroad.

'It is clear to me that the security measures around this company's access to CPR have not been good enough,' Christina Egelund, the digitalisation minister, told Ritzau. The access has been shut. Egelund has ordered a security review of the whole system and does not rule out new CPR numbers for everyone.

A CPR employee spotted the unusual activity on Friday 2 October. The case has been reported to Datatilsynet, the data protection authority, and the police are investigating. The names and addresses of people with name and address protection were not affected.
DI, an employers' organisation, says in a statement that the leak raises the risk of fraud against companies, and urges them to review their identity checks at once.

copy.headline: Government will propose bringing back an abolished public holiday in 2030

standard.text: The government will put forward a bill in spring 2027 to restore store bededag from 2030. Store bededag has been a public holiday since 1686 and falls on the fourth Friday after Easter. The plan is in the legislative programme presented on Tuesday.

Pia Olsen Dyhr, the economy and interior minister, told Ritzau the bill is timed to be settled before private-sector wage talks. The day was abolished in 2023 to help pay for defence. Under the coalition agreement, it returns only after a further rise in employment equal to the one its abolition brought. She says that will happen 'in any case in 2030'.
According to DR, employees will have to pay for the day themselves.

short.text: The government will put forward a bill in spring 2027 to restore store bededag from 2030. Store bededag was a public holiday from 1686 until it was abolished in 2023 to help pay for defence.
According to DR, employees will have to pay for the day themselves.

copy.headline: Government brings back citizenship bill for 2,055 approved applicants

standard.text: The government will bring back a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 previously approved applicants and their children in the first half of 2027, Morten Bødskov, the immigration and integration minister, said on Monday. It lapsed when an election was called.
Each applicant will first be checked again, and some may be dropped. They will not face the values screening the government wants for other applicants, which an expert group is still studying.

Venstre, a liberal party, backed the bill in February. On Monday its leader, Troels Lund Poulsen, wrote that the government should wait for the screening. Liberal Alliance, a libertarian party, calls it a 'gigantic broken promise'.

short.text: The government will bring back a bill granting citizenship to 2,055 previously approved applicants after a fresh check of each, Morten Bødskov, the immigration and integration minister, said on Monday. Venstre, a liberal party, backed the bill in February but now wants the government to wait for a values screening.

copy.deck: Each applicant will be checked again; Venstre, which backed the bill in February, now wants it to wait.

copy.headline: Dementia assessments take more than five times as long as the law allows

standard.text: In recent years 84 per cent of patients due a dementia assessment have waited longer than the 30 days the law allows, according to a report by Rigsrevisionen, the national audit office. The regions, which run Denmark's hospitals, took 165 days on average last year: 133 in Southern Denmark and 244 in Zealand.

Statsrevisorerne, who check that the state spends taxpayers' money properly, gave the regions the second-sharpest criticism on their scale. They also faulted the 24 days that patients from strong social backgrounds gain over those from weak ones.

Mads Duedahl, chairman of Danske Regioner, the regions' association, calls the criticism justified and says the field must be 'rethought'. The regions want family doctors to do more of the assessments.

copy.deck: State auditors sharply criticise the regions; patients in Zealand wait 244 days on average.

copy.headline: Human rights court says a 46-nation call on deportations will not set its course

standard.text: Mattias Guyomar, president of the European Court of Human Rights, said in a speech last week that a declaration by the 46 countries behind the court 'is not a roadmap for the court's work'. The countries, members of the Council of Europe, signed it in Chisinau, Moldova's capital, in May, seeking more freedom to deport foreign criminals.

Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister, led the push, and her government's deportation reform assumes the court will change its practice over time. 'If it turns out that the court does not change course, the new Danish rules will have no effect,' Jens Elo Rytter, professor of constitutional law at the University of Copenhagen, tells Ritzau.

copy.headline: Spain's prime minister calls an early election after losing housing votes

standard.text: Pedro Sánchez, Spain's Socialist prime minister, has called an early election for 29 November. He announced it on Monday, three days after parliament voted down two of his minority government's housing bills. 'We must renew the people's support,' he said, according to Reuters.
Average rents have doubled in about a decade; on Saturday tens of thousands marched in Madrid. The vote had been due by 22 August 2027.

Polls put the conservative Partido Popular ahead; the likeliest government would pair it with Vox, a far-right party. That would bring the far right into government for the first time since Spain became a democracy after General Franco's death in 1975.

short.text: Pedro Sánchez, Spain's prime minister, has called an early election for 29 November, three days after parliament voted down two of his government's housing bills. Polls favour the conservative Partido Popular, most likely in government with the far-right Vox.
